author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content:
Hey, I was writing my usual poem – I’ll keep it short.
I think we should avoid attracting people in their early 20s or younger. They probably wouldn’t have the patience to wait for the full release of the game.

We need to accept that we’re not a pure FPS, so competing with Web2 games in that niche is tough, which would require a first-person camera and some polish in the movement and shooting systems.

MMORPGs with FPS elements are such a hard genre to balance – just look at Anthem or The First Descendant.

In my opinion, things like lore, deep space exploration, and economics aren’t what typically attract younger players, but we could try to shift their perspective and introduce them to a new gaming paradigm. Young people struggle to keep their attention on something for more than 10 seconds   they need a faster pace content (And thanks god we are building something different from the current "meta" of gaming).

We definitely can’t force everyone to love Star Atlas, but they can create their own “planet” to play on – kind of like in Ready Player One.
But yeah I guess that’s going to take a while!

What will be undeniable for everyone is the final quality of the product, the dedication and drive of the people behind SA will be what sets it apart from AAA Web2 studios, which now only chase profit and have long forgotten what "passion" truly means.

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content: I've mostly been thinking of the FPS components as the combat style which the game will use while we're out adventuring. So I agree - I don't think SA will be a contender in the pure FPS genre.  To your point about the MMORPG / FPS fusion, I think it's a difficult one. I don't know too many people that are fans of both genres. I'm interested to see how the team plans to tackle that particular challenge.  Lots of single player games seem to do well with the RPG/FPS style (Borderlands, Fallout, etc), but those have mechanics to assist the player (auto lock, slow motion, etc) which probably don't translate well for a pvp fps setting.  With combat being such an important component of an MMORPG, I think it's important to make sure that the combat system is fun and engaging without "getting in the way".

author: (CB) RatODoom
content: Even with a large player base, you don't need hundreds of unique planets to make each one interesting. You need enough options to mix and match, then combine that with procedural generation to get something interesting. Some key planets should be completely unique and carefully developed. But I think it's totally ok to have "filler" plants that feel familiar.  You travel to a smaller desert planet, you expect to encounter things that fit that category. But the truly alien planets are those which are individually designed to be special and challenging.

I’ve seen this issue in New World (a Web2 game, so not exactly apples to oranges), and the devs eventually merged all markets in one. But if Chris and the econ team think it’s fine, then I trust them completely. They’ll likely adjust the game mechanics to "stimulate" local markets in the future.

author: mikatachan | [ROME]
content:
@[AEP] Lerinor this is just my uninformed opinion, but working through your question... what could the team actually do in current circumstances re priority fees?

at least in my head, priority fees are the same thing as gas fees on ETH. when the network gets busy, priority/gas fees go up because people are trying to get their tx through before other people, so the fees rise. it's not really something SA can control in its current form.

one solution i can think of is if the team created a solana L2, did all of the game tx there, then settled it back to mainnet on their dime. realistically, I can't even imagine the amount of work that would take, but i dunno

author: mikatachan | [ROME]
content: Oh yeah, Solana is to blame for the situation, but we inserted ourselves in it by creating a very transaction-heavy product.  And by all means, I'm not blaming or pointing fingers. Just a reality. Fees weren't an issue (old Labs is the example, we were doing what, 10% of all SOL transactions? Wild!). But now they are.  That's why I asked the question. Because most times we bring this up, someone from the team replies with "yeah, we are aware, and are working on solutions". I merely asked what are some of the ideas to counter the situation.  I personally am a big advocate for an overhaul on cycle times (even if that means some painful moments of rebalancing formulas/math/metas/shenanigans).  We're moving towards new products/features (C4, Fleet Command, etc.) and I REALLY want it to be a blast, and attract new players. But reality is, Sage is a sandbox test environment, and it doesn't reflect end product. So maybe think of it in terms of detaching functionalities? UE5 will integrate with Sage at some point? Maybe. If so, keep the fast paced/short cycles loops in UE5, and make Sage that sluggish part of the economy that is boring, supposed-to-be-automated, and make the fees impact on it be much smaller.  This is me purely theory-crafting, but I'd love to hear what are the actual solutions being worked on.

reply.preview: Oh yeah, Solana is to blame for the situation, but we inserted ourselves in it by creating a very transaction-heavy product. And by all means, I'm not blaming or pointing fingers. Just a reality. Fees weren't an issue (old Labs is the example, we were doing what, 10% of all SOL transactions? Wild!). But now they are. That's why I asked the question. Because most times we bring this up, someone from the team replies with "yeah, we are aware, and are working on solutions". I merely asked what are some of the ideas to counter the situation. I personally am a big advocate for an overhaul on cycle times (even if that means some painful moments of rebalancing formulas/math/metas/shenanigans). We're moving towards new products/features (C4, Fleet Command, etc.) and I REALLY want it to be a blast, and attract new players. But reality is, Sage is a sandbox test environment, and it doesn't reflect end product. So maybe think of it in terms of detaching functionalities? UE5 will integrate with Sage at some point? Maybe. If so, keep the fast paced/short cycles loops in UE5, and make Sage that sluggish part of the economy that is boring, supposed-to-be-automated, and make the fees impact on it be much smaller. This is me purely theory-crafting, but I'd love to hear what are the actual solutions being worked on.

content:
Transaction comes to the validator -> people in the companion app chose a validator to stack their polis with -> Validator separate transaction into pieces and send it to a X number of mobile endpoints to validate -> mobile app performs individual atomic operations and return to the validator with a response -> validator approves the state
not high cost validators, realy decentralized and hard to tamper with. The validator can delegate transactions depending on how much Polis and endpoitns staked in it
mobile app get some Atlas on exchange of their computing power
that can be used to mint crew
while they need some POLIS to peg into the validator

author: [HEIM] CapThor
content: Thank you for speaking up. The only part of the announcement that worried me was actually a pretty important one. What a lot of people have been voicing (myself included) is that the vision wouldn't be compromised by adapting Sage to new realities. If you think about it, it's pretty absurd to be able to traverse the entire known galactic map in a matter of a few hours on subwarp, with minimal fuel costs. Longer cycles wouldn't cripple the fun, especially because we're not claiming for a 20x increase. There are many ways to implement something along those lines, and I'm sure this has crossed the team's minds (and they for sure know how to make it better than many - if not all - of us). But when a hardline is drawn about adapting to new scenarios/conditions, well... it didn't ring well for me. All the rest (which is massive stuff) sounds great! But none of the options/solutions address the urgent matter of fee impact. We (SA ecosystem) are bleeding a sizeable amount of SOL/day, and it's been weeks since priority fees are at least 2x original fees to keep things minimally running. Not talking optimal, that's at least 3x on average.

author: *Solaris* 4NUNN4KI
content:
⁠archived-foundation-room⁠
For me the major concern about using an alternative layer to address the gasfee issue is the infrastructure cost to set up nodes on it and become a validator.

Delegating governance tokens to validators whose physical infrastructure is not distributed among distinct entities/people does not lead to real decentralization. And I know that this remains an essential goal for SA but that is the complexity of the problem.
In the best case scenario it could take years, and in the worst case scenario it could never happen because it would probably be difficult to find people/entities willing to become validators on a niche chain. The main interested parties would be the players themselves, and the only ones financially capable would probably be the whales.
So on the one hand we would solve a problem, but on the other hand we would add a layer of complexity in terms of decentralization.

The initiative remains commendable on paper but I am waiting to have many more details.
For the moment this is the only opinion I can give in light of what I can understand.
In any case, bravo to the team for taking this subject head on.

author: ZiggyMUD
content:
Could the design of Apollo change where blockchain value goes?

Typically a blockchain has a token for transactions and this same token is what is used to value the network. As the network becomes more valuable, the transaction cost becomes more expensive making it more costly to use.

It seems Apollo's tokenomics might be designed to change this.

My hypothetical thoughts:
Blockchain/project value goes to POLIS
Transaction costs are tied to ATLAS an in game currency that is intended to be stable, or at least tied to in-game earnings. Both the network and the game economy are aligned.
If the value of the project/blockchain increases POLIS, this does not effect the cost to transact on the network but more expensive to be a validator to validate the network. However validator earnings would also scale with game usage (network usage) in the form of trading fees, crafting fees, etc. So one would think that POLIS' price would rise with player growth and game usage, possibly with swings over priced and underpriced, however these swings should not affect gameplay or network transactions.

Star Atlas continues to upgrade its network to the latest Solana upgrade, but fixes how network tokenomics work, which is likely more of an economic problem which the ATMTA team are masters at. 

Could this also help to make in-game NFT prices more stable? Could this also make the Star Atlas economy less reliant on the crypto market cycles and more in line with the actual in-game economy?

author: diegomtxUstur
content: decentralized bridges are basically smart contracts, for example you'd lock your asset in a smart contract on solana, then the corresponding smart contract on apallo would mint the same asset. to transfer back to solana, the asset on apallo would be burned (or locked), and the corresponding contract on solana would release the originally locked asset. Nothing actually transfers from one chain to the other. but it does seem that way in practice. the security risk here is that you are introducing a complex smart contract on both chains that have significant security implications. the solana side would have a significant amount of liquidity locked in a smart contract (proportionate to the amount of assets on apallo). and the apallo side contract has the ability to effectivly mint assets (limited to apallo). Where as normally that ability is centralized to a multi sig where the signers are known.

author: mikatachan | [ROME]
content:
just throwing in my 2 cents. haven't seen this mentioned yet (or missed it), but imo implementing an L1 in Apollo would be... a huge ask and I don't think we should honestly. 

On-chain liquidity is going to be a huge problem, and fragmentation is a reason why a lot of chains fail (ie. Cosmos/Polkadot/etc). Sure, we'd be able to get transactions through faster and cheaper, but what happens if we want to swap or bridge? Do we have the current player base / liquidity / new exchanges to support all the economics required? I would say no.

Doing so just opens up a lot of risk, and I'm not sure if I see it as beneficial to Star Atlas in the long run. Short term, possibly yes, but long term I would say it's a mistake to commit that many resources to developing an L1. L2 maybe, but i dunno.

author: [SAG] Swift42 [CODE]
content:
Regarding your message in Fr @[DEEP] Digital Fists :
One reason SLY got faster: I heavily optimized the core tx functions. The new SLY version saves a lot of requests because all concurrent signature checks are bundled into a single RPC request. The more fleets you have, the more requests you save (e.g. the old version issued a request every 2 seconds per fleet, so if you have 100 fleets you had 3000 requests/minute; the new version only needs 30 requests for the same task).
This allowed me to "invest" a small portion of the saved requests into another area: a tx is now resent more often.
Reason:
With many transactions in the network queue, an initial send might get stuck behind a large backlog. While the blockhash is still valid, the transaction must still be seen and processed by validators. Continuously resending it can increase the chance that our transaction “bubbles up” to the front of processing queues.

the biggest practical implication in my eyes with moving to a independent chain is that your largely disconnected from solana. many projects go to eth for this very reason, not becasue it is cheap or fast, but becasue its a vast network with many users, utility, even the layer two's have a lot of traffic, and are fairly turnkey. solana has the users, and the liquidy/utility, but the layer two aspect is in its infancy. unlike using something like IMX on eth, we might find that building a niche and independent network like apallo isolates us from solana users, and builders.

yea the atlas or polis would be locked on the solana side, and that would allow the user to mint the sol needed on the apallo side to have a proof of stake

author: [Λ] Sawyn [BR] [STAR]
content:
@SW4GN3R and @bunthius Hi, good morning. I've been playing Deathmath and I found some things to be quite unbalanced. I'd like to share my experience and suggest some improvements.

1 - There's a weapon whose name I've forgotten now, it's kind of like a machine gun. It's very abusive. You can't play against it, especially if there's ping involved.

2 - Punabs are small and hard to hit, while Ustur model 2s are really easy.

3 - There are two types of damage, but you don't really care about which one does more damage to the shield.

Proposed balances:

1 - It would be interesting to reduce the speed at which the hail of bullets is ready to be unleashed. This would make it combatable, since if you encounter the person at the same time, you know you have a "window of time" to fight.

2 - I believe that a general rebalancing of the races would be interesting.

Change the HP of all races.

Punab (smaller ones) have 25 HP, movement speed 1.25.,Punab (larger ones) have 55 HP, movement speed 1.10.,Meriese have 90 HP, movement speed 1.0.,Humans and Sogmians have 100 HP, movement speed 1.0.,Ustur (thin) have 125 HP, movement speed 1.0.,Ustur (fat) have 200 HP, movement speed 0.70.,The shield remains at 100 points. Why these values? Well, we consider the current weapons and a fair balance. This will create different gameplay modes. Punab players know that if they get shot by a Sniper, it is certain death. On the other hand, it is very difficult to hit a shot like that. Also looking at the direct combat aspect, the Punab knows that from the moment he loses his shield, he will have to run a lot, because anything will kill him. The opposite is the fat Ustur, where he doesn't need to rush, he will be able to enter combat and be a living wall.,
Later, when the item and skill system is implemented, the shield can be directly influenced by the engineer characteristic in the future, and HP by fitness.

author: [Λ] Sawyn [BR] [STAR]
content:
3 - An alternative for a third type of weapon would be a toxin/acid weapon. First, it would further reduce the damage of physical weapons to the shield; the damage of energy weapons seems ok when it reaches HP.

Toxin weapons would act "outside the shield" directly on HP. But not in direct damage, but rather as a poison or acid that corrodes the enemy. There would be no direct cure, but there could be a "vaccine" spawn that improves the player's resistance against this type of weapon for a period of time. This weapon could have a bonus against Ustur (kind of like an anti-tank, and this was the reason for increasing the HP of the thin Ustur).

Anyway, these are ideas. I hope you consider them.

author: [AEP] Funcracker [AEP]
content:
@mirko.k I hardly know where to begin, so I asked ChatGPT to save me time and effort:

Can you answer this question related to Star Atlas' desire to be on-chain:

"hi, but why is the decentralization of a blockchain so important? In my opinion it doesn't make much sense... if a centralized blockchain can guarantee greater scalability and greater performance it is preferable to a decentralized system. Just set some basic rules in the protocol where anyone who breaks them is not validated... I have never understood the importance of this word."

Certainly! The importance of decentralization in a blockchain, especially in contexts like Star Atlas or other Web3 applications, revolves around a few key principles and benefits:

Trust Minimization
 •    Decentralization ensures that no single party controls the system, reducing the need to trust a central authority. In a centralized blockchain, the entity in charge has significant power over decisions, data integrity, and access. If this entity becomes malicious or is compromised, the entire system’s integrity can be undermined.
 •    In contrast, decentralized systems distribute power among many participants, making it harder for any one party to manipulate the system or impose biased rules.,
Censorship Resistance
 •    Decentralized systems are much harder to censor because there isn’t a single point of control. In a centralized blockchain, the controlling entity can easily block users, freeze assets, or prevent certain transactions. Decentralization prevents this by distributing control among many nodes, ensuring that no one can unilaterally censor or restrict access.,
Resilience and Security
 •    A decentralized blockchain is more resilient to attacks and failures because it doesn’t rely on a single point of failure. If one node or participant goes down or becomes compromised, the system as a whole continues to function.
 •    In centralized systems, a breach or failure in the controlling entity can compromise the entire network, making it more vulnerable.,
Open Participation
 •    Decentralization allows anyone to join the network and contribute to its operations, fostering inclusivity and innovation. In a centralized system, access is often limited or controlled by the central authority, creating barriers for users and developers.,
Immutable and Transparent Rules
 •    Decentralized systems operate on open, transparent, and immutable protocols. Everyone in the network can verify that the rules are being followed without relying on a central authority’s promises. While centralized systems can set basic rules, enforcing them consistently without bias requires significant oversight and trust.,
Alignment with Web3 Values
 •    Decentralization is a core tenet of Web3 philosophy. Projects like Star Atlas aim to empower users, giving them ownership and control over their data, assets, and participation in the ecosystem. Centralization would undermine this goal by reintroducing the power dynamics of Web2 platforms.,
Decentralization vs. Performance
 •    While it’s true that centralized systems often offer better scalability and performance today, advancements in blockchain technology (e.g., layer 2 solutions, sharding, rollups) are narrowing this gap. Many see decentralization as a trade-off worth making for the added trustlessness, security, and fairness it provides.,

Teranode resolves this by allowing the blockchain to scale horizontally and vertically, ensuring high performance without creating central points of failure.  It achieves this while preserving the fundamental decentralized nature of the network, ensuring trustlessness, censorship resistance, and inclusivity.   In short, Teranode bridges the gap between performance and decentralization, providing a decentralized system capable of supporting enterprise-level applications like Star Atlas without sacrificing core blockchain principles.

author: Buzzec
content: Is this what you mean? I'm not crazy technical but believe the community should understand all the tech ATMTA is building. Not everyone will care, but it will be important for those that do.  Seamless Upgrade: The upgrade wasn’t designed to introduce flashy new features but rather to improve compatibility and ease of use behind the scenes. Ideally, users wouldn’t notice because everything continues working smoothly, but better.  Support for Standard Wallets: The upgrade ensures that any wallet extension adhering to the standard wallet adapter (likely the Solana Wallet Adapter standard) will now work automatically across the Star Atlas ecosystem. Developers don’t need to write custom integrations for every new wallet.  Benefits for Developers and Users:  Developers: If they create a new wallet extension that meets the standard, it will immediately work across all relevant Star Atlas products without additional effort. Users: They can use a wider range of wallets seamlessly, as long as the wallet meets the standard. Simplifying Integration: The update focuses on making the ecosystem more flexible and compatible. By adhering to a shared standard, any compliant wallet will function across the board, making it easier to onboard new wallets and users.  This is a technical but significant quality-of-life improvement for both developers and the community, even if it isn’t immediately visible to users.

⁠archived-foundation-room⁠ @[-U-] Orionorbit the tricky part with this idea is that the discovered stash needs to be "worth" more than the fuel (+tx fees) that it requires to get there and back. author: [SAG] Swift42 [CODE]
content:
I see some potential problems with your idea: @[-U-] Orionorbit 
If there is an incentive to use small ships to get airdrops, I guarantee that someone will program a bot or extend SLYA to benefit from it - sooner or later. (and tbh, I don't think it would be very hard to program a bot for it)
Because the formula is simple: When there is money to earn, players and programmers get super creative. It's the same thing in other games where an account can e.g. only earn 0.01 USD/day. Just make 1M bots and boom! you earn 10000 USD/day. I mean, players even program bots in games where you can't even earn money.
There is no way to implement something where only small players benefit from, because big players can just "emulate" small players (e.g. with automation and/or multiple wallets).
If you increase the ROI of a small fleets by giving small players special airdrops, why even use/buy big fleets then? SA would cut into its own flesh.
And you would even need to prevent things like: I'm a big player and I use 1M SDUs. I find 100k airdrops in 100 different sectors. So in each sector I have now 1000 airdrops - a LOT of RSS per sector. I can just use a big fleet to pick up all airdrops. Easy peasy. 
So you would need to prevent that a player can get multiple airdrops at once. But I could circumvent it with multiple wallets and automation.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: Agreed with Swift on this.  The only surefire way to have small player only "manual" gameplay is through UE5.  That's exponentially more difficult to bot and to bot in scalable numbers is near impossible.

author: Xap✨ [STAR]
content: I thought you meant that the use of an SDU will give you a chance that a lootbox is dropped for you somewhere and the lootbox is bound to your profile. But when your idea is to randomly drop lootboxes and a SDU scan reveals a position, then it raises another problem: All data is on the blockchain. While you can somewhat obfuscate things (like the SDU chance in a sector), you can't hide the information that someone gets about a loot box position. So some other player can just read the blockchain, find out the position and snatch the lootbox. So you end up with no loot.

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content: Will there already be APY projections of locked polis for validators in the addendum?   I believe that in order to attract investors interested in blocking their polis there must be more favorable conditions than the return that polis on Dao has.   Otherwise investors would have already locked in Dao.   What I mean is: if I had to lock my polis to become an Apollo validator, I would only do it if the apy was fairly higher than what I could get from Dao (currently mine are around 3% per month locked for 4/5 years )  If the validators APY wasn't high enough, I would continue to keep my polis unlocked.  Otherwise I would have blocked them already in Dao.   So in summary I think the APY would initially have to be very attractive to work. My opinion.   or will the block of polis be unique and this will provide two cumulative returns?   So for example, I who already have the tokens locked in Dao will also be entitled to an additional apy as I would also automatically become a validator?   This would lead to the monthly return of the locked polis becoming really interesting and would probably naturally attract a good number of new investors and locked polis.

author: [AEP] Moustacheride
content: TTBH. People still do not understand Apollo and its role as defined my MW and SA team.   To understand it fully one has to think out side of the box. For example, people still believe that SA need to have a separate token to be used in Apollo. That is not the case. Apollo will use Sol. It will use Atlas for compensation/commission and Polis for stakes.   Some of this still needs to be expanded, evolved and described but this is what has been shared so far. Granted what I have written here can be changed by the time the team posts further details about Apollo.   For a current player the experience will be same as using the Port of Entry to move assets from Solana to Apollo.  A number of these pieces already exist.   Yes it will take much more development to get it be fully functional but it is not 3-4 years of development. A centralized initial version is achievable depending upon scope and resources within an year. It is very doable.   All of this is speculation by me based on information provided so far and my experience leading and building tech products for decades.

Low risk: doesn’t interact with inflation of resources
Movement: 3tx+ (undock, warp, dock)

Transport: 5tx+ (load crew, undock, warp, dock, unload crew)
fleet management (form / disband 
Starbase cargo (withdrawing / depositing cargo)
Port of entry (import / export)
marketplace (local and galactic)

content: Well, that is one way that was discussed (but not all that much by the team tbh).  I really like this approach as well. Keep as much as possible on Solana, but have the game run on Apollo. Use the Port of Entry as a locking mechanics on Solana, to release assets (real, or virtual) on Apollo.  On Apollo, new assets (beyond those arriving through the PoE) would be created non-stop, through mining, scanning and crafting, and then destroyed when moved to Solana through the CSS. Moving things out of the game would unlock them on the Solana side, or create them if they weren't there.  Of course, when something is destroyed in-game (combat), the asset (e.g., ship) is destroyed on Solana as well.  Then, if we make Atlas Prime mandatory on Apollo, allowing you to bridge ATLAS from Solana directly into the ATLAS Vault, and vice-versa, the process will become more complex, but it would still feel pretty seamless.  If something like this could be achieved, it would be near invisible to people that the actual game is running on a side-chain. Moving things out of the game would unlock them on the Solana side, or create them if they weren't there. Of course, when something is destroyed in-game (combat), the asset (e.g., ship) is destroyed on Solana as well. If something like this could be achieved, it would be near invisible to people that the actual game is running on a side-chain. author: mikatachan | [ROME]
content: They are taking about using the port of entry as the bridge point. Which makes sense since it’s already a gateway of sorts.   Basically there’s a bridge and another chain. The other chain operates independently so the bridge is where the magic happens.  The bridge normally uses one of two methods: liquidity pools, or smart contracts. Smart contracts being the decentralized option. Liquidity pool would look something like the point of entry on the Solana side sending your asset to a pool controlled by the team then you’d be able to withdraw that same asset on the Apollo side from a separate pool in game. (You see this when using a cex to bridge assets) deposit btc to binance, and now you can swap to eth and withdraw. You’re effectively interacting with pools of assets on both chains and trusting Binance.   The alternative is smart contract. Where you’d lock the asset on Solana side in a smart contract, then that contract would work in tandem with another smart contract on Apollo to allow you to release the same item in game. Bridges by no means transfer the asset from one chain to another.

author: mikatachan | [ROME]
content: Can’t awnser fully, but based on the convos with the team in this chat, and the brew I can say: 1) validators compensated by the dao primarily (Swagner said this in the initial announcement) 2) polis would be used to determine eligibility(also in the announcement) I imagine it would also be used as the proof of stake token. 3) they are leaning towards port of entry as the bridge point. I think this would exclude the galactic market, so we’d be able to have new users buy assets there initially, if Apollo captures local market they would have to bridge that atlas or earn it in game before using it. 4) assuming point of entry is the bridge point, sage would be on Apollo, everything else would not.  5) bridge security is one of my concerns. Centralized bridges rely on liquidity pools and the security protocols of that central (or small group) that controls the pools. Smart contracts don’t have the liquidity pools, but they do have significant amount of assets locked up in the contracts on both sides. If there is a smart contract exploit then it can be leveraged. Decentralized (contract) bridges are considered higher risk because of this. Hacking a centralized liquidity pool requires getting access to the account with the permissions, whereas a smart contract can be leveraged by anyone who finds a vulnerability.

author: Xap✨ [STAR]
content: RE: Multi-accounts  I think this is only really a problem if it provides some sort of PvP advantage. It's really difficult to speculate right now because there are so many unknowns. For the sake of discussion, let's run with an example of open space combat.  Multi-accounting only provides an advantage if multiple accounts can get involved in a particular scenario. For example, if we have a system where combat is initiated and this opens a window for multiple people to join - there's an advantage to anyone with coordination and fast response time, so a rather significant advantage to a multi-accounter.  This can be mitigated through engagement mechanics - simply don't allow multiple parties to join that battle.  It can be mitigated through progression design - require human focus for meaningful progression.  It can be mitigated through combat mechanics - incorporate some active component to combat.  Note that none of those would affect multi-accounters from an "economic warefare" perspective. It's not enough to just say "we want to prevent/deter multi-accounting". We have to define a specific action or scenario where there is a risk of multi-accounting providing an unfair advantage, and then we can suggest mitigations which reduce/remove that advantage.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: Yeah, when CR comes out, we will uncap XP, because the CR itself will serve as an XP cap based on scale of your operation. I actually think CR has greater potential to negatively impact revenues, as it won't make sense to bring a million dollars into the game on day one -- but at least it combats the "pay to win" narrative. And it is a more fair system, in line with all of the original game design. Also, the XP curve in early game should be quite friendly. I/we don't have any specific numbers yet (though Chris has been working on it, so we might have an initial version), but the exercise is going to involve determining what level of play and XP progression gets most people into their desired fleet in a reasonable amount of time. Purely hypothetical, but can a player bring $500 of assets in on day one? Maybe. And within the first week, perhaps they can level up sufficiently to grow that to $2500 or $5000, should they want to buy that many ships.   Separately, in terms of new players being hamstrung because of competition, I also don't really see that as a consequence. With the map expansions coming in C4, there will be a lot more to do in SZ (not to mention, some protections through game mechanics in MRZ). And in every MMO, you learn the game and level your character in a starter area that is usually quite easy. So that's where I envision new players embarking on their leveling and fleet expansion activities.

author: questionoak
content: A VAT type tax system would mean lower DAO revenue but the big question is the million dollar Reaganomics question... Do lower taxes improve the economy? If a person buys iron ore paying in the cost 6%, then converts to iron, then sells paying in the cost 6%, then person who buys makes a framework and sells in the cost 6%. The last 6% is obviousl the highest tax revenue for the DAO. If the others got their taxes back, the last tax is still the largest tax payer. The VAT idea is to stimulate trade and tax final products.

author: [SAI] Lollo | lollo.sol
content:
Guys, girls. On behalf of the Atom team we want to thank you all for your interest and for sharing your valuable early feedback. 
We are very happy to have started this discussion with you today! Launching this closed beta marks an important milestone for us: providing you with a testable version of Atom to try out while we focus on your thoughts, suggestions and ideas. We’re ready to tackle it all, bring it on!  

As mentioned earlier, we will do our best to listen to your feedback and incorporating your suggestions to make Atom an even more complete, competitive and efficient tool.

We understand that fees are a topic we still need to refine and opening Atom to you is an essential step in finding the ideal solution. Despite this, we hope you’ll dive in, explore and appreciate the incredible work that our devs are doing to make concrete what was only a dream in the drawer. 

We want to emphasize how much we value your input, all feedback is welcome. We’re excited about the journey ahead and can’t wait to move from this closed beta to the public launch.

Hey folks! Love the convo and love that ATOM is close to launching 

Anyone allowing a hot wallet to be controlled by someone else is running the risk that their assets won’t be doing what their owner intended.

author: [SAI] Lollo | lollo.sol
content:
Thank you @[AEP] Funcracker! We’re thrilled to have started the release of Atom in closed beta!  

I completely agree with you on the importance of clarifying that Atom hot wallet with permissions allow fleet basic movements (load/dock/start mining, etc..) inside SAGE. 

However, it’s very important for us to make a few clarifications. 

Regarding the topic of an attack by SAI The key point I’d like to emphasize is that Atom is NOT a product of SAI. While it was created by members who are part of SAI, Atom is an independent product developed by a passionate and independent team called Hexon. In the future, as we grow, it’ll be amazing to onboard talented people from other backgrounds! About the topic of attacks or misuse, as you’ve also pointed out, it’s obviously not in our interest. Doing so would destroy all the work we’ve done in an instant, for what purpose?

Regarding Atom in the cloud. As @[SAI] Sim has already explained in a message above, Atom in the cloud is the SaaS solution for Atom. Atom, however, is structured in two parts: Atom SaaS (everything cloud-based and accessible through our website, that is the product you’re currently testing) and Atom Core, Atom’s automation engine that abstracts many of the complexities of the SAGE library and will be made open source. Atom Core will be a product aimed at the community and designed for those who want to build their own automation systems or contribute to its development. Additionally, we will provide documentation on how Atom SaaS works, along with some API endpoints and as many resources as we can to bring the most value to the community.

author: [SAI] Lollo | lollo.sol
content: In other words, Atom Core will be the perfect product for anyone who wants to build a home automation system without going through the Cloud version and it will be released simultaneously with the public release of Atom SaaS

author: ! ᚺEIM | VɪᴋɪɴɢᴇɴBᴇɴɴʏViking
content:
About the chatter above in regard of gaming. I think its difficult because our long term target audience is the traditional web2 space. And i think people here in web3 forget how hesitant, toxic and stubborn that audience is towards new technology. I challenge you to play an online web2 game and mention crypto to see reactions  

Star Atlas being unique 100% on chain (which is why i came here in the first place) does invite a ton of challenges i think many dont realize yet. As of late people realize the danger of fee's in order to play, thats just one major issue. 

It also needs to invite unique gameplay that stands out. Currently there's nothing that really stands out to our main target audience even when polished, cause well it all excists in web2 and the competition for that audience is fierce. We need something really special in terms on gameplay, not just tech wise but gameplay, cause gamers dont give a shit how things work on the backend, just as long they can have a good time. Can we provide a good time in the future? I def think so but there are many things that needs to hit the spot  for it to happen.

Also part of the convo above kinda shows how our current audience works. Normally the gaming content creators live and breathe the games out of pure passion having thousands of hours in a game. I myself had 3000+ hours in my fav games before i got wife and kids But when it comes to web3 its mostly about money, web3 gaming content creators shifting towards ai and hyped stuff cause well money is their passion. And this is where web3 and web2 really clashes, many dont realize it but is what it is. A web 2.5 solution is currently the best option to having success in blending the two audiences at this point. Alot of projects chose this path so they should be successful, right? Well their gameplay tend to be shit or so basic its not fun or worth digging into the .5 aspect of the web 

Sorry bout the rant but thats how i see it. Ive been here for years and truly hope this succeeds as we all wish, but we also need to face what problems lie ahead of us so we can solve them before its all over cause we all ignored them

author: ! ᚺEIM | VɪᴋɪɴɢᴇɴBᴇɴɴʏViking
content: We need those fun gameplay loops and I think the two different mindsets will thrive off of each other. The people driven by money and economic loops will drive and incentivize the fun gameplay once it exists. Major combat and war will be driven by money and power and control over resources. The guy who wants to dogfight will find his fun in the chaos. The people who like to run freight will have opportunities to support the front line and supply chains. The people who like the mining and/or crafting loops the same. Bounty hunting same thing, the money will drive the demand. Hunting for animals and creatures? Same. It can all tie together I think. Even people who just want to venture off and do their own thing. Exploring caves and ruins for a shot at a rare item? They’ll be a market for everything imaginable, people will own everything they do. Of course the team has to create these loops and most of all make it enjoyable and fun which money itself can’t fix.   I think when we reach the point where we can have combat in Ue5 and have the results of battles be from individual players skill instead of an algorithm that it’ll become super fun super fast. Still many challenges tho like the txn issues

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: My issue and highlighted in bold so as not to be confused is this is NOT a PROJECT. It wasn't meant to pick on your use of the term because I hear it a lot in here. I wasn't try to pick on you specifically. I probably also should have been more correct and used the term DAO instead of COMPANY, but in most jurisdictions they are treated as companies (in Wyoming they are actually treated as LLCs). A DAO is an organization - be it a non-profit corporation or for-profit corporation - this is NOT a PROJECT.  In the governance docs going back to 2021-22, the term "assets" is used throughout.  Accounting 101... Assets=Liabilities+Equity.  Every time we convert USD to USDC and send it into the marketplace, we are investing in the DAO. I stand behind that statement and I would be surprised if the DAO's accounting firm sees it any other way. We are exchanging fiat (USD) to digital asset (USDC) to digital asset (C11). That is GAAP. Throughout all the docs dating back to the beginning we talk about building a virtual economy based on these digital assets. I think we need to remember that we are building an economy (NOT A GAME). Every economy in the world wants to attract investment. And this comment is not directed to anyone in particular but the fact that I get shot down when I want us to talk about bringing in investment into this economy makes my point that we need a channel with the big boys that want to talk about real USD coming into this economy.  Meanwhile my offer to lend real world asset servers bought with real USD to the DAO for free is still on the table if they can help. Maybe they can be used to fix some of the ailments of this economy until a way for the economy to pay for RWA servers is devised.
